section_summary: This section documents tightening concern over Japanese access to petroleum and other strategic materials during mid-1941, including gasoline, crude oil, cotton, manganese, beryllium oxide, tungsten, antimony, quartz crystal, leather and agricultural exports. State Department correspondence records negotiations with oil companies, reports from diplomatic posts, export-control deliberations and American press demands for an oil embargo. The final portion contains a large group of public protests sent to Interior Secretary Harold L. Ickes, reflecting anger that citizens were being asked to conserve fuel while petroleum continued to reach Japan or Vichy-controlled territories.

subfiles.title: Telegram on a Brazilian letter of credit for Argentine mice exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports financing for the export of mice from Argentina to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Bank of Brazil opened a $10,000 letter of credit in favor of Alcaid Hermanos of Buenos Aires. The transaction covered mice for export from Argentina to Kakehi and Company in Japan, and the telegram was repeated to Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Letter on outstanding licenses for under-87-octane gasoline exports
subfiles.about: Provides intelligence on petroleum companies' licenses and plans to supply Japan with lower-octane aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: The writer reports that Pacific Coast suppliers had largely exhausted their licenses, while Cities Service allegedly shifted Gulf licenses to Pacific Coast shipments for Mitsui. Republic Petroleum reportedly held licenses for about 250,000 barrels sold to Nissho and was seeking Pacific Coast supplies before the licenses expired. The letter warns that these outstanding licenses could permit another supplier to provide 86-octane gasoline to Japanese interests in China.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Parker's petroleum-export letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of information about petroleum-product shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks Parker for his July 18 letter on petroleum exports from the United States to Japan. Pages 324 and 325 are duplicate or near-duplicate copies of the same acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese press reaction to prospective oil restrictions
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese newspaper interpretations of American statements concerning oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo evening papers prominently reported the President's remarks on oil exports and Acting Secretary Welles's statement to Ambassador Nomura. Most interpreted the remarks as advance notice of an oil embargo, although a Yomiuri correspondent characterized the President's tone as unusually moderate.

subfiles.title: Corrected figures for Indian raw-cotton exports to Japan and Shanghai
subfiles.about: Corrects an earlier report and supplies June cotton-export figures.
subfiles.summary: The sender states that a July 24 report was erroneous because it relied on an inaccurate story circulating in Bombay. June exports to Japan totaled 60,361 bales from Bombay, 21,994 from Karachi and 5,000 from Tuticorin; additional figures are supplied for shipments to Shanghai from Bombay, Karachi, Calcutta and Madras.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Argentine strategic-commodity exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to British data on Argentine strategic exports to Japan in the first quarter of 1941.
subfiles.summary: The sheet describes the referenced document as forwarding first-quarter data on strategic commodities exported from Argentina to Japan. The original was filed under the defense series rather than reproduced here.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese attempts to buy Netherlands East Indies sisal
subfiles.about: References a conversation about Japanese efforts to replace restricted Philippine hemp with sisal.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum recorded a conversation with a counselor of the Netherlands Legation. It concerned Japanese attempts to purchase sisal in the Netherlands East Indies because of American restrictions on Philippine hemp exports.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Banco Minero wolfram shipment to Japan
subfiles.about: References a Bolivian report on efforts to ship wolfram to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The subject line, though damaged by OCR, concerns efforts by Banco Minero to ship wolfram from Bolivia to Japan. The original communication was filed in the defense records.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Heavy movement of strategic materials from the Americas to Japan
subfiles.about: References an internal memorandum recommending action on strategic-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum described a continuing heavy movement of strategic materials from the Americas to Japan. It also suggested that action be taken in response.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Great Lakes Carbon Corporation correspondence
subfiles.about: References transmission of a Great Lakes Carbon Corporation letter and a request for instructions.
subfiles.summary: The OCR-damaged subject indicates that the Department transmitted a copy of a letter involving Great Lakes Carbon Corporation. It apparently requested guidance on whether a proposed transaction or reply should proceed; the original was filed under defense regulations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese acquisition of Brazilian quartz crystal through objets d'art
subfiles.about: References information on Japanese attempts to obtain Brazilian quartz crystals disguised as art objects.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch concerned Japanese efforts to obtain Brazilian quartz crystal through purchases of old objets d'art. The original was filed in the defense series.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Japanese Embassy note
subfiles.about: References a Japanese Embassy note whose subject is largely illegible in the OCR.
subfiles.summary: The page points to Japanese Embassy note number 134 dated May 20, 1941. Only fragments of the subject, including a reference to customary courtesies, remain legible, so the precise matter cannot be established from this section.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Bolivian tungsten and antimony shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: References data on June shipments of Bolivian tungsten and antimony to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to telegram 157 from Jenkins in Bolivia. That telegram supplied data on tungsten and antimony exported to Japan during June.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese purchases of Brazilian manganese
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese manganese shipment from Brazil and attempts to obtain additional parcels.
subfiles.summary: The British source reported that Mitsui and its agents had booked space aboard the Arabia Maru for 1,000 tons of Brazilian manganese of 43 percent content. The firms were also negotiating for freight space on the same vessel for further purchases.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on a Japanese offer for Argentine beryllium oxide
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese offer to buy the entire production of S.A.B.A. for three years.
subfiles.summary: A secret source in Buenos Aires reported that Japanese buyers offered to take S.A.B.A.'s entire output for three years at 27 Argentine pesos per kilogram, free on board Buenos Aires. Dent suggested that the report justified an early decision on proposed American purchases of Argentine beryllium oxide.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of report on S.A.B.A.
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Dent's report concerning the Japanese offer for S.A.B.A.'s production.
subfiles.summary: Finletter thanks Dent for his June 6 letter. He specifically identifies its subject as the Japanese offer to purchase all of S.A.B.A.'s production.

subfiles.title: Proposed telephone response to Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Proposes guidance for responding to Standard-Vacuum's request about gasoline for Japanese forces in China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that supplying gasoline from sources outside the United States was not prohibited by American law, so the government would not formally oppose the transaction. It nevertheless says the government would be pleased if Standard-Vacuum declined the Japanese request, while leaving the final commercial decision to the company. A handwritten notation indicates that this position was telephoned to the company.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with A. G. May on gasoline for Japanese forces
subfiles.about: Records Standard-Vacuum's request for guidance on supplying 86-octane gasoline to Japanese forces at Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: A. G. May explained that Standard-Vacuum had voluntarily applied American export restrictions to supplies from the Dutch East Indies and had resisted Japanese pressure for aviation fuel. The company feared that refusal would provoke tighter restrictions on its Yangtze trade, while compliance could contradict its prior claims that the fuel was unavailable. Hamilton and Adams said the transaction was legal but inconsistent with American support for China, leaving the decision to the company and declining to promise retaliation based on a single case of Japanese interference.

subfiles.title: A. G. May letter on Japanese gasoline and aviation-oil demands at Shanghai
subfiles.from: A. G. May, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Forwards company cables showing that Japanese authorities linked Yangtze trade permits to supplies of aviation-grade fuel and oil.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai requested authority to quote on large quantities of 86- or 74-octane gasoline and aviation engine oil for Japanese forces and airlines. Company representatives warned that refusal could end permits for shipments to Suzhou, Nanjing, Wuhu, Hangzhou and other Yangtze markets and expose Standard-Vacuum to further retaliation. May emphasized that the company had made no commitment and requested the Department's views before deciding.

subfiles.title: Telegram summarizing American press opinion toward Japan
subfiles.to: U.S. Embassy Tokyo via Shanghai; repeated to Chungking and Peiping
subfiles.about: Summarizes recent American editorials on an oil embargo, Japan's Axis alignment and U.S. policy in East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports continuing editorial demands to end petroleum exports to Japan, including criticism from Texas newspapers. It quotes the New York Times warning that cooperation with Hitler would make Japan dependent on Germany and that the war in China was an exhausting failure. Other editorials range from hope for cooperation to calls for a firmer American policy and skepticism that any agreement with Axis-aligned Japan could be trusted.

subfiles.title: Texas newspaper clippings opposing petroleum exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Condemns continued American oil and gasoline sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Austin clipping argues that Japan's conduct has made its promises and motives untrustworthy and that petroleum exports should end. The Waco clipping calls it irrational to conserve fuel domestically while supplying Japan's war against China and possible southward expansion.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping: “What Next for Japan!”
subfiles.about: Warns Japan against deeper cooperation with Hitler or expansion into Russia and the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: The editorial describes Japan's China war as an impoverishing failure and criticizes military ambitions toward the Netherlands East Indies and Russia. It argues that Hitler would exploit and ultimately subordinate Japan just as he turned against the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping: “America and Japan”
subfiles.about: Sets out conditions for peaceful relations while warning Japan against continued aggression.
subfiles.summary: The editorial rejects Japanese hopes that transfers from the U.S. Pacific Fleet signaled weakness. It says Japan could avoid dependence on Hitler by abandoning conquest and accepting equal trade for all nations in China and the Western Pacific.

subfiles.title: Clippings on Japan's possible strategic alignment
subfiles.about: Discusses whether Japan would follow its Axis role or find cooperation with the United States more advantageous.
subfiles.summary: One clipping argues that Japan was being pushed by the Axis to obstruct American aid through pressure around Vladivostok or the Netherlands East Indies. The other suggests that Japan might instead cooperate with Russia, Britain and the United States because its interests were not wholly aligned with Germany.

subfiles.title: Hamilton Journal-News clipping: “Quicken Our Pace”
subfiles.about: Calls for faster defense production and a firm American position in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The editorial urges increased production and aid to Britain despite Germany's war with Russia. It argues that defense spending is futile if the United States simultaneously allows Japan and other dictatorships to expand without resistance.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Australian leather reexports through Shanghai to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports uncontrolled Philippine reexports of Australian leather believed destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Philippine dealers were importing substantial quantities of Australian leather shoulders and bellies and freely reexporting them to Shanghai because the materials were uncontrolled. Manila opinion held that much of the leather then went to Japan, and samples showed that the shoulders were suitable for shoe soles.

subfiles.title: Telegram announcing export controls on leather shoulders, necks and bellies
subfiles.about: Replies that the forthcoming export-control schedule will cover the reported leather products.
subfiles.summary: The Department responds to Manila's August 1 telegram. Export Control Schedule No. 16, effective September 10, would include leather shoulders, necks and bellies, with a copy sent by airmail.

subfiles.title: Recommendation to control exports of leather shoulders and bellies
subfiles.about: Recommends placing leather shoulders and bellies under export-license control.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses a paraphrase of Sayre's Manila telegram describing Australian leather moving through the Philippines and Shanghai to Japan. In light of that information, he recommends adding the materials to the controlled list.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Manila telegram on Australian leather
subfiles.about: Restates the report that uncontrolled Australian leather was moving through Manila and Shanghai to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase says Philippine dealers imported important quantities of Australian shoulders and bellies and reexported them without hindrance to Shanghai. Local opinion held that much was then sent to Japan, and examination showed the material to be of good quality and suitable for soles.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley's referral of John L. Hanson's oil inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's inquiry about a broadcast alleging that Britain guaranteed unlimited oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wiley encloses John L. Hanson's letter for attention and reply. He requests a duplicate report that he can transmit to Hanson.

subfiles.title: John L. Hanson letter on an alleged British oil guarantee to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions a broadcast report that Britain had guaranteed Japan an unlimited petroleum supply.
subfiles.summary: Hanson asks why Britain would supply oil to Japan while the United States was sending resources to Britain and restricting other supplies. He fears that American aid could indirectly equip a potential enemy and notes that he had not seen the allegation discussed in the press.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Wiley
subfiles.about: States that the Department has no evidence of a British guarantee of unlimited petroleum supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply refers to Wiley's August 2 letter and Hanson's enclosed inquiry. It says the Department has no information suggesting that Britain made the reported guarantee and returns Hanson's letter.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese pressure for continued Bolivian mineral exports
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese threats to withhold textiles unless Bolivia reserves minerals for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rumors indicated that Japanese interests were trying to secure a portion of Bolivia's mineral output by threatening to end textile exports. The message was conveyed informally through German representatives or Japanese trading houses rather than through the Japanese chargé. Jenkins believed Bolivia would resist and noted efforts to obtain a larger quota of British textiles.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator letter forwarding public protests
subfiles.from: Ralph K. Davies, Office of Petroleum Coordinator
subfiles.about: Forwards communications protesting petroleum exports and a list of their authors.
subfiles.summary: Davies explains that the Interior Department lacks authority over petroleum exports and has told correspondents that export policy falls within the State Department's jurisdiction. Pages 369 and 370 are duplicate copies of the covering letter, while page 371 begins the extensive list of protesters whose communications were attached.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on jurisdiction over petroleum export policy
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department was properly described as responsible for petroleum-export policies and regulations.
subfiles.summary: Reed records that Adams had delivered Davies's August 4 letter after Peck studied the jurisdictional statement in it. Peck apparently concluded that responsibility lay with the Administrator of Export Control under the Act of July 2, 1940. Reed asks for confirmation that can settle Adams's concern.

subfiles.title: Continuation of list of petroleum-export protesters
subfiles.about: Continues the names and addresses of people who protested petroleum exports.
subfiles.summary: This page continues the list associated with Davies's August 4 forwarding letter. It records correspondents from New Hampshire, Vermont, California, New York, Connecticut, Colorado, North Carolina, Washington, Georgia, Ohio, Minnesota and New Jersey.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of petroleum-export protester list
subfiles.about: Provides a duplicate, more poorly reproduced copy of the list of anti-export correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The two pages substantially duplicate the names and addresses appearing on pages 371 and 373. OCR corruption is extensive, but the list again identifies citizens and civic representatives whose protests were forwarded to the State Department.

subfiles.title: A. M. Stonehouse letter with clipping on oil for Japan
subfiles.about: Challenges domestic conservation appeals while the United States supplied most of Japan's petroleum.
subfiles.summary: Stonehouse asks why Americans should conserve oil while, according to an enclosed New York Herald Tribune article, the United States supplied more than 60 percent of Japan's petroleum. The clipping reviews American and Netherlands East Indies oil shipments, the limited effect of partial embargoes, Japan's dependence on imported oil and the risks of an attack on the Indies. Page 378 duplicates or enlarges part of the clipping and includes fragments of neighboring international-news items.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Lasalle Felheim letter to the Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: A largely illegible handwritten protest concerning petroleum policy.
subfiles.summary: The surviving handwriting is too poorly recognized to recover the complete argument. Its placement among the forwarded protests and the legible question “why” indicate that it challenged current oil policy, particularly continued exports while conservation was urged at home.

subfiles.title: Stephen H. Fritchman letter supporting an oil embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Offers to support gasoline conservation if the government completely stops oil shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fritchman congratulates Ickes on efforts to conserve domestic gasoline and supports freeing tankers to aid Britain. He argues that Americans would accept voluntary reductions more readily if assured that none of the saved fuel would be shipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Henry E. Rice letter opposing gasoline shipments to Vichy France
subfiles.about: Urges the government to stop tankers carrying gasoline to Vichy-controlled France.
subfiles.summary: Rice reports hearing that two tankers were loading gasoline for France at an eastern port. He argues that domestic shortages already made the shipment unwise and that Vichy assurances could not prevent the fuel from being diverted to Axis military use.

subfiles.title: W. C. Wright letter questioning gasoline conservation and exports
subfiles.about: Questions asking motorists to conserve gasoline while aviation fuel was allegedly sent to Vichy France.
subfiles.summary: Wright asks what purpose conservation serves if high-quality aviation gasoline continues to reach the Vichy government and potentially the war against Britain. He invokes his long association with the Pennsylvania oil business and warns that public knowledge of the policy would cause outrage.

subfiles.title: W. S. Wheaton handwritten protest
subfiles.about: A poorly legible protest concerning American petroleum policy and Germany.
subfiles.summary: Only fragments of the handwritten note are intelligible. In the context of the accompanying protest file, Wheaton appears to question policies that conserved fuel domestically while allowing supplies to assist foreign aggressor powers.

subfiles.title: Mrs. William R. Van Buskirk letter with “Foreign Magnates” clipping
subfiles.about: Criticizes conservation appeals without an embargo on petroleum exports to Axis powers.
subfiles.summary: Van Buskirk argues that complaints about domestic gasoline waste are unpersuasive while large quantities are exported to Japan and other aggressor powers. She calls for an embargo and contrasts the export policy with criticism of domestic “profit” or waste. The enclosed Paul M. Deac column alleges that American and British oil interests replenished German and Italian supplies through the Canary Islands and sold roughly 900,000 barrels monthly to Japan.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Waldo A. Amos letter on oil shipments, Vichy and domestic rationing
subfiles.from: Florence K. Amos (Mrs. Waldo A. Amos)
subfiles.about: Questions fuel shipments connected with Vichy North Africa and asks for clear domestic gasoline-use guidance.
subfiles.summary: Amos asks Ickes to explain reports that tankers of oil were going to aircraft in North Africa, citing Weygand, Vichy and German activity near Dakar. She expresses support for President Roosevelt, comments critically on Lindbergh and discusses possible bases in Dakar or Gambia. She also asks for a definite gasoline allowance for motorists and says her disabled husband's recreational driving could be surrendered if necessary, but not merely to provide more oil for Japan or Vichy France.

subfiles.title: Louise Moody Merrill telegram protesting oil policy
subfiles.about: Fragmentary telegram associated with Merrill's protest against petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Only the telegraph form, date stamp and a few damaged characters survive on this page. The accompanying correspondent list identifies Merrill as having sent both a telegram and a letter, and the following pages contain her fuller protest.

subfiles.title: Louise Moody Merrill letter opposing oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests supplying Japan with oil while Americans are asked to conserve.
subfiles.summary: Although the handwriting is poorly recognized, Merrill clearly objects to oil being used to help Japan kill others while the American public is asked to make sacrifices. She questions the policy's logic and urges that petroleum shipments be stopped.

subfiles.title: Mrs. L. B. Taylor letter on fuel conservation and civilian hardship
subfiles.about: Objects to threatening domestic fuel restrictions while Japan might continue receiving petroleum.
subfiles.summary: Taylor asks whether Americans are expected to accept reduced heating so that Japan will not suffer, noting that an invalid aunt could freeze during the winter. She suggests using railroad tank cars and argues that repeated threats of shortages damage public morale while citizens already struggle with taxes.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Alfred W. Stone letter protesting oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls domestic gasoline conservation contradictory while oil exports to Japan continue.
subfiles.summary: Stone contrasts newspaper appeals for conservation with statistics showing large recent oil exports to Japan. She sarcastically suggests that using more gasoline might keep it from Japan and calls the policy a cruel joke because the fuel could eventually be used against American servicemen.

subfiles.title: Joseph A. Shirley letter asking who supports oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests an explanation of the policy and asks where effective appeals to end Japanese oil shipments should be directed.
subfiles.summary: Shirley condemns supplying oil that Japan was using against the Chinese and might later use against American soldiers and sailors. He also argues that the United States could need the petroleum itself and asks who was responsible for the policy and where protests could be made effectively.
